# Plan: migration (cockpit to oculus)

Execution ledger for `tools/oculus/DESIGN.md`. One bullet is one package of work and one agent dispatch, except the bookkeeping packages the orchestrator does itself (marked). A package is ticked only after its verification commands ran and the orchestrator read the whole diff; the commands are in `orchestrator-state.md`, and nothing is ticked on inspection. The green checkmark is this file's status vocabulary by Axel's instruction of 2026-09-10; everything else in this folder is ASCII. Read `orchestrator-state.md` first after any context compaction. The lettering C, R, S, O is the ledger's own; the cockpit roadmap's letters A to I map onto the O packages as noted.

One key cannot hold both kinds of entry, so the point cannot be built under the name ruling 297 gives it. Nothing else of ruling 297 changes: `en` shipped and the default, the workspace setting `settings: { language: <id> }` (a key apart from the reader's option `languages:`, the extension-to-language map of `config/defaults/sources.yml:81`), the English word for a key the language lacks, a finding for a key oculus lacks, and `settings: text:` laid over the chosen language. (a) VS Code's own point for a display language, `localizations`, in VS Code's shape: each entry `{ languageId, languageName, localizedLanguageName?, translations: [{ id: oculus, path }] }`, the path a folder of files with the keys of `config/text/`, and `settings: { language: <languageId> }` choosing one. Pros: the name and the shape VS Code gives a language pack, as the rule that VS Code parity is exhaustive asks; `languages` keeps meaning a programming language. Cons: `translations` is a list whose one id oculus reads is `oculus`, so an entry is longer than ruling 297's. (b) an oculus name, `displayLanguages`, each entry `{ id, label, path }` as ruling 297 wrote it. Pros: ruling 297's entry unchanged. Cons: a point VS Code does not have, beside the one VS Code has for the same job. (c) the display languages under `languages`, and VS Code's programming-language point renamed. Pros: ruling 297's words kept whole. Cons: every app that registers a programming language breaks, and the point no longer matches VS Code's. Recommended: (a), VS Code's name and shape for the job. (b) is the lazy option: it keeps the ruled entry by inventing a name instead of taking VS Code's point. Left for Axel: the choice is between the name ruling 297 gave and the VS Code parity rule, a clash between two of his rulings. Part (2), raised 2026-10-24 on Axel's question whether the workspace setting also follows VS Code: VS Code has no display-language setting in `settings.json`; its Configure Display Language command writes the choice into the runtime arguments file `argv.json`, and its command line takes `--locale` (code.visualstudio.com/docs/configure/locales). `localizations` is only what a language pack contributes. (a) the workspace setting is named `locale`, its value the `languageId` of an installed `localizations` entry, kept in the workspace file where ruling 297 puts it. Pros: VS Code's word for the choice, and no clash with `language`, which oculus's settings already use for a programming language (`editor.languages`, `config/options/behavior.yml:311`). Cons: changes the key name ruling 297 gave. (b) `settings: { language: <id> }` as ruling 297 says. Cons: one word for two things in the same settings. Recommended (a); (b) is the lazy option.
